utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mathias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. Before we call the witness into the courtroom, I would like to address the Defence with regard to the memo that they sent us concerning the witness schedule for the following week, that is to say, the week on the 22nd, 23rd, 24th, 25th. The Judges have noted that this memo doesn't contain the list of exhibits that you might want to show the witnesses. I would like to remind you that when the Prosecution called its witnesses, they always attached to their memo a list of the exhibits that had either tendered or would be tendered. Defence counsel hasn't indicated exhibits that they want to use that have already been admitted, nor have they indicated the exhibits that they will be tendering. It would be in interest of justice to have -- to be familiar with the exhibits you intend to show before the witnesses come. The witnesses are here to support your case, but if you don't present the exhibits before the witnesses come, this will make it a little more difficult for everyone to follow, for the Judges to follow, for example. It's in the interests of justice to do this in advance. You may continue to proceed in this manner, but in the Judges' opinion, it would be more beneficial if we had at least a list of the exhibits that have already been admitted into evidence and that you intend to use unless when drafting your memo you are not in a position to know which exhibits you will be using. That would be a possible explanation. In addition, in December, a witness will be testifying for a number of days. This is something I have already said, but I will repeat it. The hearing on Monday, the 6th of December won't be held because the Judges will be having a Plenary Session. So this witness, the witness scheduled for that date, will not be able to testify in the first week of December -- or rather, he will only be able to testify as of Tuesday, the 7th of December. I wanted to point this out to you. As far as the exhibits are concerned, is there anything the Defence would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we are trying to comply with all our duties in accordance with the Rules and the instructions of the Chamber. We try to do even more than we are supposed to do to make it easier for everyone to follow the proceedings. We know that for the last two months of the Prosecution's case, the Prosecution provided us with a list of the exhibits they would be using for the witnesses they called. So far, the list of exhibits that we'll be using have been provided to the Prosecution so that the Prosecution could prepare itself. Your Honour, we understand that you would like to have this list as well, and we will provide such a list to the Trial Chamber, too. There are certain problems for which it is not possible to provide a list of exhibits at the same time as the list of witnesses. The main problem is that the translation department provides us with translations a little too late. As you know, there are many documents in our list that haven't been translated, and I have to say that we still haven't received translations for the first witness next week. We hope we will receive these translations today, and tomorrow morning we will be able to provide the Prosecution with a list of the documents we intend to use. Naturally, before we see the witness, we cannot know for sure whether we will use all the documents that we intend to use because it's only when we see the witness that we can determine which documents we can show him or her. As far as we are concerned, we will carry out our obligations. This is in the interest of our client, and naturally I think this is in the interest of expeditious proceedings. We try to provide the Chamber and the Prosecution all the documents that we intend to use on a given day so that we don't waste time on looking for documents in the course of the proceedings. As far as the witness you mentioned is concerned, the witness who will be heard in December, we will provide the documents, the relevant documents, two weeks in advance, and we hope that the translation department will give us by tomorrow the translations of all the documents that we intend to show this witness. So by Tuesday at the latest, the list of exhibits we intend to use, or rather the list of exhibits that have already been admitted into evidence will be provided both to the Prosecution and to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that information. Is there anything the Prosecution would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you for the floor. We note simply that we don't as of yet have a list of any documents for the witness tomorrow, which again is more of a pressing concern in the immediate future than next week. We would be grateful for any indication as to which document or documents might be used with tomorrow's witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Defence counsel, as far as the witness scheduled for tomorrow is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we'll be seeing this witness this afternoon. For the moment, we haven't got the intention to use any particular document. We have provided this information to the Prosecution. However, if some material should be used, we will inform our colleagues from the Prosecution of the fact by 5.00 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll call the witness into the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I'd first like to check that you're receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please say "yes, I understand you."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you testify, I'd be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names, your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Hamid Suljic. I was born on the 25th of April 1970 in Zagradje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently I am unemployed, but I'm a locksmith by profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you have a profession of any kind? Did you hold a position of any kind? And if so, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wasn't employed, didn't work before 1992 or after 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, were you assigned to a military unit of any kind, and if so, which unit were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 93rd, yes -- in 1993, yes, I was a member of two units. That is to say, I was a member of the Mehurici Detachment, and towards the end -- just a minute. Are you referring to 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I was a member of the 314th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a rank in the 314th Motorised Brigade, or did you have a function of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the commander of the 3rd Company of the 4th Battalion in the 314th Motorised Brigade. There were no ranks at the time, but there were some sort -- there were markings, a yellow marking and a blue one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993? Or is this the first time that you will be testifying about these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the witness said he was a machine fittest, not a locksmith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will have to answer questions that will be put to you by Defence counsel for the accused. As a rule, Defence counsel may conduct their cross-examination for up to an hour and a half. After this stage, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will also ask you questions. As a rule, their examination-- cross-examination will last the same amount of time as the examination-in-chief. After the Prosecution has cross-examined you, Defence counsel may re-examine you. Their questions should be related to the questions put to you by the Prosecution. According to the Rules, the three Judges sitting before you may ask you questions at any point in time. Usually, the Judges prefer to wait for the conclusion of the examination-in-chief and cross-examination before they ask witnesses questions. The Judges should have enough time to ask you questions that they think they should ask you in the interest of justice if both parties don't go beyond the time allocated to them. Try to answer the questions precisely. If you fail to understand a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. The Judges don't have any written documents that relate to your testimony. As a result, your testimony is very important as you will be giving oral testimony, and your answers will be providing us with the necessary information. Try to be as clear and precise as possible. If you don't know the answer to a question, just say so. I'd also like to provide you with two other pieces of information that are very important. Firstly, and this is very important, you have taken the solemn declaration. You shouldn't give false testimony because false testimony is an offence for which you could be given a prison sentence of up to seven years. So this is something you should bear in mind as it is an important factor. Secondly, I would like to provide you with some information about the answers you will be providing. If you feel that an answer could be used against you, you may refuse to answer the question. But if you refuse to answer a question, the Trial Chamber may oblige you to answer it. In such a case, you're granted a form of immunity which means that what I saw cannot be used on a subsequent date against you. This Rule exists in order to ensure that witnesses feel free to testify in the interests of truth. If you encounter any difficulties, please inform us of the fact, and we will try to resolve them. Your testimony should be over by the end of the day. I'll now give the floor to Defence counsel who will provide you with some additional information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Suljic. As the Presiding Judge has just said, there is something else I would like to draw your attention to. As we both speak the same language, you might want to answer my questions immediately. However, it is necessary for my questions and your answers to be interpreted in order to enable everyone present in the courtroom to follow what is being said. This is why I would be grateful if you could make a brief pause after I have put my question to you, and only then answer the question. Mr. Suljic, where do you live right now?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I live in the Mehurici local commune, in Miletici, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, could you tell us where you lived at the beginning of the war in 1992, or rather in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I have always lived, since the time of my birth, that is to say, since 1970, in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were a machine fittest. Could you tell us something about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I completed the first four classes of primary school in the Zagradje primary school. It's not a big school so the last four classes, the 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th class I finished in Mehurici. And I completed secondary school in the Dautovic school in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told the Chamber that you were not employed before the war. Just before the war, what were you involved in? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Since the area is a mountainous one, and the people were involved in agriculture, raising livestock, et cetera, before the war although I had completed secondary school -- secondary school for machine fitters, I was involved in raising livestock and agricultural work. I worked with my parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Suljic, did you serve in the army before the war; and if so, which army did you serve in?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I served in the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you obtain a rank in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the school for reserve officers in Bileca, in the school for infantry, I was conferred the rank of corporal. We then went to serve in Pancevo, and after that we went to serve in Sombor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina is over, do you still have a rank of any kind?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the end of the war in 1994, by decision from the presidency, I was promoted to the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, at any point in time after the beginning of the war, did you join any defence units? And if so, which units and where?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, when the Serbs arrived in the Meokrnje sector, in the Zagradje local commune, we formed a local village unit whose task was to go on patrol in the village to provide security for religious buildings, for the water supply system, et cetera, because at the time there were no such lines. So that was the first time I became engaged in what would later become the BH Army. That occurred in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the units you referred to Territorial Defence units, or did they belong to any other armed forces?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: How would you I put it? These units were village units. Later they became part of the Territorial Defence. Or rather, they part of the Mehurici sector staff. At the time it was called the Zagradje company, which was part of the Mehurici sector staff. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, did you have any duties in that company in the sector staff?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I was an ordinary private. Naturally, since I had graduated from the school for reserve officers, I also had the opportunity of becoming a platoon commander. After the formation of the sector staff, I was appointed as an operations officer in the Mehurici sector staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, what sort of weapons did you and your troops in the unit you were part of have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, I didn't have any weapons. But my father did. He had a pistol. Since he was involved in raising livestock, he had a license for a 7.62 millimetre pistol. This is the pistol I would carry around with me. Members of those units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you move a little back from the microphone because it is difficult for the interpreters to hear you clearly when you speak directly into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The troops at the time had hunting rifles and carbines because we didn't have any other weapons. We only had the weapons that our local inhabitants had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, in 1992, in the summer of 1992, were there any organisational changes within the sector staff? And if so, tell me which unit you then became a part of?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the sector staff was formed, and then detachments were formed. My unit became part of the Mehurici detachment at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the command of your detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The detachment command was in the elementary school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What duties did you have in the Mehurici detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: In the Mehurici detachment, I was the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Suljic, in the year 1992, as a member of the sector staff, and later on the Mehurici detachment, did you participate in combat operations? And if that was the case, where was that?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first combat operation that I took part in was the Meokrnje operation. I participated in that operation together with my Zagradje detachment. I was on the right flank of those forces that launched an attack on the Meokrnje facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were the operations officer in the Mehurici detachment, where did you spend most of the time and what activities were you engaged in?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, and during my engagement in the Mehurici detachment, I spent most of my time on the line. The Defence line that I was deployed at was at the Zenica River and the Bila River. My task was inspect every trench, every dugout. Our task was to reinforce the defence lines and the defence positions. My task was to control the way the trenches were dug, to give the instructions to men, to have the dugouts constructed for the men to take shelter from shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, when you were not in combat, you and your men, did you go to any barracks? If this was not the case, what would happen with the men who were not on the defence line?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: We are talking about 1992. There were no barracks. There was no accommodation for the troops. We did not have any conditions for that. Members of my unit would spend time at home once they returned from the lines, when they were on leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, towards the end of 1992, were there any significant organisational changes in the BiH Army? If that was the case, could you please tell me, if you know, what changes took place?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I had towards the end of 1992, brigades were established. Towards the end of 1992, the brigades were established, and my unit, together with the unit to my left, were incorporated in the 314th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the command of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: According to my information, although I did not have an occasion to visit the command, I received the information that the command of the brigade was in Zenica, in a street called Travnicka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your duty or position at the time when you became a member of the 314th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of December 1992, if I'm not mistaken, I was the commander of the 3rd Company of the 4th Battalion of the 314th Motorised Brigade. This is the Zagradje Company I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, where was the command of the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The command of the 4th Battalion of the 314 Motorised Brigade was in the elementary school in Gluha Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you became a member of the 314th Brigade, did your battalion have the barracks for the troops?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The battalion did not have any such thing. However, in the area covered by my company, that is, in Zagradje and in the Gluha Bukovica elementary school, there were a platoon in each of these buildings. 10 to 15 members of each platoon had a task to intervene on the defence line should there be an attack launched by the aggressor or a unit of the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, you have told me that you resided in Miletici village at that time.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me who you lived with in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I lived with my family. To be more precise, my father, my mother, my three sisters and my two brothers. In Miletici, there were also other members of my family. To be more precise, three of my uncles. That was in Donja Miletici. There is also a village called Gornji Miletici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who resided in Gornji Miletici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: In Gornji Miletici, the population was Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your relationship with your neighbours from Gornji Miletici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Our relationship was good. We visited each other. We socialised. We spent holidays together. They celebrated Christmas. We did it together with them. We celebrated our holidays. They celebrated those with us. Whenever there was a party, whenever there was a funeral, we would visit each other. In addition to that, for example, we were each other's best men. We participated in every aspect of each other's lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, in the year 1992, in addition to the population that resided there already, did the refugees start arriving in Mehurici and in that general area? If that was the case, can you tell us where they came from.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The Bila valley and Mehurici became the gathering point of refugees from all the over the place. Most of them came from the relation of Banja Luka and Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, did you notice at any point in time that some foreigners started arriving in your area? Foreigners who did not hail from either Bosnia-Herzegovina or the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such foreigners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where these people came from? Did you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: It is very hard for me to say where they came from. I was not a policeman. I did not inspect their IDs, so I wouldn't know where they came from. Some of them had fair skin. Some of them had dark skin. And I wouldn't be able to tell you where they came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see foreigners wearing typical uniforms of Arabic countries?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them. I saw them in Mehurici, in the Mehurici mosque. Friday is the church day for Muslims, and it was on a Friday that I saw these people for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your first encounter in the mosque, did you later on see these people in some other places?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I saw them in the mosque, but I also know that they were in the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Mehurici elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they accommodated in that elementary school? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The sector staff or the Territorial Defence - I'm not sure which one of those organisations - was on the first floor of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you and other people call these foreigners? And how did they themselves introduce themselves to the people of the area?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: At first, we just called them Arabs. We didn't know who they were. However, later on, it turned out that they came from other states of the world. At the beginning, they introduced themselves as humanitarian or aid workers. They brought presents and aid to the population because the conditions at the time were really very bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the name that people used for them changed?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: People watched television, and they saw reports on Afghanistan where the word mujahedin was mentioned. So people started referring to these foreigners as mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to one thing that I've already asked you. When you mentioned their accommodation in the elementary school, can you please tell me where the command of your detachment was, in which part of the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The detachment command was in the staff room. This is where we had our briefings. This is where we had our meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the staff room on the ground floor or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: It is on the ground floor, to the left, the first door to the left as you enter the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw, heard that these foreigners had arrived, where were they accommodated in the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: They were on one of the upper floors. There are two upper floors. I never had an occasion to go upstairs to visit any of these floors, so I wouldn't know exactly on which floor they were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. You've told us that at the beginning they introduced themselves as humanitarian workers, that they distributed all sorts of aid and presents amongst the population in light of the dire straits that the population was in. Mr. Suljic, are you aware of the fact that these foreigners had left the school? And once they did that, where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: First they were in the school, and then they left. As you cross the bridge in Mehurici and you walk by the mosque and you start climbing uphill towards Poljanice, there's a place called Savica house. I believe that the family name is Savic. And this is the house where they found their accommodation later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once the brigade was established and once your detachment was incorporated in the 314th Brigade, where was the command of your company?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: It was in the elementary school in Zagradje, in the settlement called Luka. That is where my company command was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in a new position. In that position, did you learn anything about the possible problems that these foreigners may have caused in your area?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was during a religious service in Mehurici. The Efendi informed people about the problems that we had with these foreigners, these mujahedin. What was it all about? First of all, they introduced their way of observing religious services. In Bosnia, we have Islam, but we practice it in one way. And they came from different parts of the world, and they started introducing their own customs. And that's where the first problems arose from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, at that time, did you know that in addition to these problems that involved religion, and despite those problems, that there were still people who joined them?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know of anybody joining their ranks. It was maybe later on that people started joining them, but this was mostly for training. Some lads who were still minor and who were not members of the BiH Army joined them for some sort of training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your village, in the village of Luka, were there any particular problems? Or let me ask you: Was your unit in any contact with these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No. We did not have any contacts with these foreigners. We had our own mission, our own task, which was primary to defend the line that the command of our unit entrusted us with. We didn't have any problems with them. They caused problems in Mehurici and in Kljaci. This is where they created most of the problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your information, how did they behave towards people who did not want to follow their religious ways and customs in those two places that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: There were even some threats against people who did not want to observe their ways. It was very difficult during that period of time for people to go to a mosque. My late uncle, who was 80 years of age at the time, he always rebelled. He said my father taught me one thing, and now all of a sudden, there are these new people who are now teaching us new customs. At that time, it was very difficult for the people to observe the religious teachings of Allah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, let's now move on -- let's move on to a very specific event. Can you please tell us where you were on the 24th of April 1993, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of April 1993, I was on the defence line at the forward command post of the 3rd Company in the area of Studenac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is this defence line from your command post in Luka village i.e., how far is it from Miletici, from the place where you resided?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Some 15 kilometres or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, on that day, did you leave your combat position, and were you supposed to -- or did you go back to your command?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Once my task was accomplished at the forward command post of my company, I went to pay a visit to the forward command post of the battalion. Then I went to the forward command post in Gluha Bukovica. From Gluha Bukovica, I went home. Actually, I was walking towards Mehurici settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend any time in Mehurici, or did you continue towards your command post?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't spend any time there. I asked a colleague of mine who had a car to drive me to my command post, to the company command in Luka elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were travelling, did something happen? Did you have an encounter with some people? If that was the case, can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. As we started driving from Mehurici, in Celamov Gaj, I came across a column. In the column, there was my father, my uncle, my father's uncle, and my Croat neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these Croat neighbours from?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: They were from Miletici. They were walking from Miletici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there somebody with these people, or were they walking of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: They were in a column. They were walking in twos, in couples, and there were masked people around them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they walking? First of all, let me ask you, were there only men, or were there women there as well?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: There were both men and women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe how they walked? How did the men walk? How did the women walk?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Men were in the front and women were behind them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about these masked people? What did they have with them?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I saw that they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw your father among these people. Can you please tell us your father's name; and secondly, can you tell us if you Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond saw something on him.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: My father's name is Akif. And I could see blood on his right or left side. I'm not sure of the side actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about you? Where were you at that moment?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I wore civilian clothes. I wore a pair of jeans, and I had a vest that I had been given as a unit commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you armed at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was armed. I had a 7.62 millimetre pistol under my arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The masked people who were escorting your father, your family, and your neighbours from Miletici, were they armed? If yes, what arms did they carry?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The first two that I saw walking in front of the column, I saw that they carried automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the people in the column tied?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: All the men were tied, save for my uncle who was not tied. As for the women, I don't know. I did not see whether they were tied. I was focussed more at the front of the column because my father was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to approach the column? Did you try to ask anything?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did try to approach the column. However, the two people wearing masks, one of them said something in a foreign language to me. I didn't understand. But then he waved his hand, and I decided to step back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you heard this word "Yallah," did it mean anything to you? Could you maybe decide who these people belonged to?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, when I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sorry. If I may just object, my learned colleague, you just mentioned that a person has said something. I quote "Yallah" here from the transcript, and I couldn't see the witness saying that before. This would be leading.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is the interpreter's correction. The interpreter did not mention the word "Yallah" the first time the witness used it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It is not in the transcript. Let me ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, did you try and approach this column, and did somebody react in any way?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The first soldier reacted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I understood him saying "Yallah," and I don't know what this meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This word uttered by this armed man, did it cause any sort of opinion as to who this man belonged to?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I could only assume, bearing in mind that he didn't speak our language, that he belonged to the so-called mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you stepped back. And what about the column? Where did the column go to? In which direction?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The column went on towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, what did you do, Mr. Suljic?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I waited in Celamov Gaj for about 15 minutes. After that, I set off in the direction of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report to anyone in Mehurici, or did you notice something strange, anything strange in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I didn't report to anyone. I entered the primary schoolyard. And opposite the road from the primary school, there were cafes. I saw civilians coming out of the cafes. They were drinking coffee and sitting there. A soldier of mine said that they had taken his uncle and father, and his uncle Haso away. He said that the mujahedin had taken them away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how events unfolded in Mehurici? Do you know anything about the sequence of events, and do you know whether anyone attempted to get your father, uncles, neighbours released? I'm referring to the people who were taken away by the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. They tried to establish contact with the mujahedin in many ways. It was difficult to know who was in charge. That is to say, it was difficult to know who the Emir in that unit was. That's what they called the leader. Naturally, during that period of time and in that area, the person in command of those units, or rather, the person who was in command of the troops wasn't present. They wanted him to come and to talk to the representatives of the mujahedin. I know that he went there. I know that Ribo Sulejman went. I don't know that he negotiated with them. He's an inhabitant of Luka near Zagradje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, how long did these negotiations last? And do you know what the result of the negotiations was?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: These negotiations lasted for an eternity for me. A minute was a year for me. And a year an entire century, as one would say. But between 2200 hours and 2300 hours, they agreed on something. I don't know. But later, I saw my father and my older uncle in the courtyard of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, I apologise, but I just want to go back to a previous question. When you said you didn't know who the commander of that unit was, the commander of the unit in the school, which unit were you referring to? Who was in the school during that period of time? Which unit was located in the school?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, a unit of the 306th was there. I don't know which battalion, but it was one of the battalions of the 306th Brigade. It used to be called the Siprage Battalion. I think that it might have been the 1st Battalion, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go on. So around 2200 or 2300 hours, your father and your uncles were released. Mr. Suljic, tell me, do you know whether negotiations continued and what happened to your neighbours from Gornji Miletici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The negotiations were never interrupted. After my father and two uncles had been released, the people involved in the negotiations requested that the inhabitants of Miletici be released as well. I think that Ribo Sulejman played a key role in these negotiations, and naturally the commander of that battalion in Mehurici. They reached an agreement according to which these people were to be released. Naturally, these people were released up there, and they came to the courtyard. They arrived before the courtyard of the Mehurici primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And afterwards, where did these people go or where were they taken to?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: There was a bus in the courtyard. And these inhabitants of Miletici were taken to Luka by bus. So it was across the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, where did you go on that evening?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Since the situation was such as it was up there, since people were afraid, I wanted to go home naturally. But no one spent the night in that inhabited place up there. But later, I returned to the Luka sector where these people had been accommodated. I tried to visit those neighbours of mine. And naturally, I spent the night in the school in Zagradje. I wasn't able to sleep, but that's how one puts it. It was a difficult day. I was supposed to celebrate my birthday on that day, and it was the most difficult day for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, on the following day, what sort of information did you obtain and did anyone arrive in that area?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: On the following day, naturally we visited these people. To the extent that it was possible, we aided them, gave them some tea and coffee to drink, provided them with some food. And perhaps -- well, I'm not sure whether it was in the morning or in the afternoon, but vehicles arrived. I think UNPROFOR and other vehicles arrived, and some TV channels, et cetera. I don't know who else arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the foreigners who were UNPROFOR members, did you notice the presence of army members or HVO members?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that bend that led towards Miletici and in the direction of Luka, these vehicles came to a halt. And since it's about a hundred metres from where these inhabitants were accommodated, we went to see what was happening. And naturally, I saw someone with HVO insignia for the first time, and I saw another man who had the insignia of the BH Army. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond This person introduced himself, and I think his name was Dzemal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had seen these people, did any of them address you, and did you provide them with information?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dzemal said that some sort of a mixed or joint commission had come to establish what had happened in Miletici. I said that I was the commander of the company in Zagradje, and he issued -- or he gave me an oral task so to speak. He asked me whether I had any forces. I said I had about 15 soldiers. The task was to send them to the defence line. He said that these men should provide security for the civilians who were in Luka. And he said that they should prevent people from entering the village and looting property, the property that belonged to those inhabitants. Naturally, we did what we were told to do, to the best of our ability, but he also requested that I and some other soldiers go to Miletici and that we determine what had actually happened on the site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you carry out this second task, and with whom did your soldiers go to the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Look, I know that I went there in a vehicle, and there was an armoured vehicle of some kind, a vehicle that belonged to monitors, I think. I got into that vehicle and went up there. There were three or four soldiers. A shortcut was used to go to Miletici from Luka. And naturally, I went up to that area in Miletici with those soldiers. And since I was afraid -- I was afraid of what might happen. But later, it was established that there were dead people up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this commission left, could you tell me how you continued to carry out the task that the member of the army, his name was Dzemal, assigned to you?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, look, as far as the civilians are concerned, we carried out this task in a professional way because the inhabitants of Luka won't allow anything to happen to them. They were neighbours with whom we lived. On a number of occasions, the people called the mujahedin tried to enter the inhabited place in the afternoon. We wouldn't allow them to enter the place. So I think that we carried out the task to the extent it was possible for us to do so. Dzemal naturally said that we should set up a checkpoint at the entrance from Luka. He said that two men should be at a checkpoint, and they should prevent certain vehicles from entering. Vehicles that were used by men who might want to loot the property of Croats should be prevented from entering. That's what the task was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, did you carry out this task, too?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in time, did any other teams of foreigners arrive, and did the inhabitants of Gornji Miletici leave Luka and with whom did they leave?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. An UNPROFOR team arrived, and they collected the bodies which were taken away naturally. But I don't know where. Later -- well, naturally, they spoke to the inhabitants. And some of them said that they wanted to leave the area because they were afraid of the mujahedin. They wanted to go to a safe place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether these people left and where did they -- which place did they leave?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, they left Luka. Or rather, they left the houses they were in, Smajo's house, Osman's house, Idriz's house, these were the houses that they left. How should I put it? The troops escorted them to Mehurici, and there were vehicles waiting for them in Mehurici. They got into the vehicles, and they were driven away. Naturally, some of those inhabitants remained. I think Marko's family, Markinica, remained. Srecinica, Zdravkinica, I didn't know their real names. We used their nicknames. For example, Pero, we called his wife Perinica. I wasn't really interested in their real names, so I didn't know their real names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After most of your neighbours from Gornji Miletici had left, who took charge of protecting the village and the other inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: After these inhabitants had left, the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, took over the duty of taking care of the remaining families. Police patrols would visit this place on a daily basis because I know that some such people came on one occasion and had coffee in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the families that remained in Gornji Miletici are concerned, did they continue to communicate with your family and the families of your uncles? And what was the attitude of your family towards these people, towards these families?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, look, they remained in contact. They never said that we had done anything to them. They said that other people had done something to them. We were on good terms with them. We gave them food. I remember that my father would give them cigarettes. He didn't want us to take money for those cigarettes. And in that place, because they were afraid in their place, a lot of them would spend the night in our house. And in the early morning hours, they would have to go to their places to prepare food for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, did you speak to your father about this event at that time or later on?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, look, at that time my father really didn't like to talk about these things. And later on, he didn't want to talk about this. All he said was: "My son, it wasn't possible to provide help and something bad happened." That's all he said. Why did he say that? Well, I believe that he had been hit by a rifle butt, with a rifle butt when this took place. And perhaps that's why he didn't want to speak about this subject, because he was afraid that I might do something reckless and might provoke a conflict with those forces, with those mujahedin who were very dangerous in our area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Suljic, let's now move on to another subject, another event. On the 7th of June, did you receive from your battalion commander a task ordering you to go somewhere with your company's troops?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: On the 7th. Well, look, a courier arrived from Gluha Bukovica. He arrived in Zagradje. Or rather, he arrived at the unit command and said that our task was for one of our units to go via Miletici and Jezerci, Cukle, and to link up with forces from our brigade who were arriving from the direction of Zenica. That's the task he said we had to carry out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 8th of June in the morning, did you start carrying out that task? And if so, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: All the tasks that the superior command assigned to subordinate units were carried out to the best of our ability. And from the Luka sector in the early morning hours, perhaps at about 3.00 or half past 3.00, we set off from that sector, via Miletici, via Donji Miletici, Jezerci, and we continued to the Rakin Do feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that trip, did you notice whether there was any fighting in the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice anything of that sort. It was early in the morning, perhaps at 3.00 or half past 3.00 in the morning. And later on, at about 4.00, you could hear small-scale shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far did you get, Mr. Suljic, and what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I reached Rakin Do, and I was going down towards the Strazbica feature. I think that's the name. And at about 4.00 or half past 5.00, while there was shooting going on, as we were going down, and on that occasion I was wounded. I was hit by a fragmentation bullet, or rather there was a shell that fell, and I hid behind a sort of heap. Some bullets were fired, some shots were fired, and a fragmentation bullet hit me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken afterwards?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, since I couldn't see anything with my left eye since that eye had been hit, two of the soldiers took me back up to Rakin Do, and we then descended to the Jezerci village. There was some sort of reception centre, if I may put it that way. They bandaged my eye, and then they took me to Mehurici. In Mehurici, I was seen by someone called Suvad, a Dr. Suvad. And since you couldn't get to Zenica via Ovnak and the territory down there, I was returned to an area near Zagradje, and I was Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond taken along the Jasenica River via Javor to Kustarica [phoen]. And from Serici, from the village of Serici, which is in the Zenica area, I was driven to the hospital in Crkvica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, I have two other questions for you: Tell me, the families of your neighbours from Gornji Miletici, do they now go to Miletici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. They come to Miletici. They have property of their own there. And we buy hay from those people. We use it to feed the sheep, the cows, et cetera. They visit their properties, and there was a woman who came to pick the apples. A young man who went to school with me, his name was Philip, he came to see me about a month ago and had coffee with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these people come to the village, do they visit your families, and what sort of terms are you on today?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, when they come, they do visit them, if they have time, of course. Look, you're asking me about what sort of terms we are on. We're on the same sort of terms that we were on before the war. We respect each other. We respect their religion. They respect ours. So I think that even today, we treat them fairly, and they treat us fairly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Suljic. Mr. President, this concludes my examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is now 10.25. We will have our break, and we will resume at about 10 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team, do you have any questions to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We do have a couple of questions for the witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Ibrisimovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Suljic, at the beginning of your testimony, you said you were born in Zagradje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Zagradje village, there's no elementary school, is there?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The elementary school is in Luka. But Luka belongs to the local commune of Zagradje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your company was in Zagradje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Zagradje, but to be more specific, it was in Luka because there's no school in Zagradje. The upper part is called Zagradje, and the lower part by the river where the school is, that's Luka. The whole area, both Luka, Skomorje, and other settlements make up the local commune of Zagradje. In Zagradje itself, there's no school as you have just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May or June 1993, was there the 309th Mountain Brigade from Kakanj staying in Zagradje?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that unit. In Zagradje, there was only the 314th Brigade. Actually, the 3rd Company of the 4th Battalion. And that was the only unit that ever came to that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time, was there maybe a unit or the 3rd Battalion from Kakanj belonging to the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, there were no such units in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would kindly ask the witness to be shown Prosecution Exhibit Number P564. I have this document in B/C/S. Maybe it is going to make things easier if this document could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read the document?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this document, it says that the 309th Mountain Brigade from Kakanj will be staying in the school in Zagradje, and also one company of the 7th Muslim Brigade from Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Zagradje village is mentioned. However, I don't know whether there might be several places bearing the same name in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know that this particular unit never existed in my territory, and it never stayed in my area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have read the document, you can see that the municipal staff of the national defence of Kakanj should have been informed.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The municipal staff of Kakanj. But what did we have to do with Kakanj? If we're talking about Travnik, then we didn't have anything to do with Kakanj. This is relative to the units that stayed in the territory of Kakanj. I really don't know. I suppose that there must be a place with the same name with a school. This village here, Zagradje, did not have a school. There was only a school in Luka, so this letter could not have referred to us because it doesn't mention my unit at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the units are mentioned in this document that stayed in the territory of Kakanj, and if I told you that in the municipality of Kakanj, there is a village bearing the same name, Zagradje, you will agree with me, won't you?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I will, because that is a very plausible option. I even heard that there was a place called Mehurici in the territory of the Municipality of Kakanj. And as you know, there is Mehurici in the territory of the Municipality of Travnik as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We won't need this document any more. Let's go back to the incident in Miletici. When returning from the command of your battalion on that day, you arrived in Miletici, and you encountered this column in which your father and other members of your family were. Tell us, please, when you encountered these -- this column and those armed men, did you notice a member of the 7th Muslim Brigade among those masked men?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No. In that area, the 7th Muslim Brigade never existed. It was never there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am referring to that specific event when you encountered that column. Did you notice or observe any member of the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't know that they were ever there. They would have had some insignia. These persons did not bear any insignia that related them to any army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you descended to the area across the road from the school and when you were waiting for the outcome of the whole situation, in front of the school and anywhere around the school did you notice a member of the 7th Brigade or an officer of the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I only saw members of the 306th Brigade who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question at the end: On the 8th of June in the morning, you were seriously wounded. You lost your right eye.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A day before, you received from the command of your unit in Gluha Bukovica a mission or a task to go to Miletici, Jezerci, and Cukle. That was the direction where you had to go?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, not towards the village of Cukle, but above it towards the facility called -- actually, we went from Luka to Miletici, and then from Miletici -- Donji Miletici towards Jezerci village, and then Rakin Do. Rakin Do was our final destination and there we linked up with the forces that were moving from the direction of Zenica. And it's -- I was informed well at that time those were the units of the 314th Brigade that were moving from the direction of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, you have the floor. Cross-examined by Mr. Neuner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Suljic. My name is Mathias Neuner, and I'm representing the Prosecution here, and I'm going to put a couple of questions to you. If you don't understand my question, please ask me to rephrase it, and I will try to do so. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, apart from your JNA service, you were living all your life in Donji Miletici or in Zagradje where you stayed at Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the school. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Donji Miletici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the family name Suljic which was a common name in Donji Miletici, were there other families by the name of Suljic in the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were people bearing the name Suljic in Zagradje. I'm not aware of any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I take you to your own name, Hamid Suljic, to the best of your knowledge, do you know that any other person by the name of Hamid Suljic was living in the Bila Valley in 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't be a hundred per cent sure. I have never seen any population census, so I have never been in the position to see whether there was any other Hamid Suljic living in the Bila Valley. I was the only Hamid Suljic residing in the Bila Valley, in Miletici. I can't be sure of anybody else bearing that name residing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You know Halim Husic?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Halib Husic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Halim Husic, he was in 1993 assistant commander in the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he was born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I cannot tell you where he was born. He testified in front of this Trial Chamber, and he stated that in 1993, he was in Rudnik and working there at the command of the 306th Brigade. Would this help you?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: If you're talking about Halim Husic, the one from Dub, then I can say that he was a theology teacher, a religious education teacher, and I do know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is exactly the person I'm talking about. He studied in Saudi Arabia -- I'm not exactly sure, but in an Arabic country. So you know Mr. Halim Husic. You were a colleague or a friend of Mr. Halim Husic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to object to one part of this question put to the witness by my learned friend. When he was explaining where Halim Husic studied, the witness said that he was a student in Sarajevo. And I don't know where my learned friend got this information from, that he was a student somewhere in Saudi Arabia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: To the best of my -- to the best of my recollection, the witness has appeared some weeks ago. I just knew that he was travelling to the region, and I wanted to help actually Mr. Suljic to remember Mr. Halim Husic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if I understood correctly, you said he was a professor of theology. Do you recall whether he was studying in Sarajevo? I think you already stated Mr. Husic, but can you please tell the Trial Chamber whether you know Mr. Halim Husic from Sarajevo -- whether you know he was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: How am I supposed to know where somebody graduated from? I was not interested in that. I only knew that he was a theology professor, and I also know that he worked in Sarajevo. Now, as to where he graduated from, I really wouldn't be able to tell you that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Halim Husic in 1993 from time to time?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him in Mehurici in the mosque on Fridays during the religious service, the main religious service that usually takes place on Fridays. And he would be there. He would often come there to participate in this religious service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, can you state the name of this mosque, please, in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: It doesn't have a name. Our mosque was just the Mehurici mosque. In Zagradje, there was the Zagradje mosque. So our mosques bear the names of the settlements. Our mosques do not bear any other names. Those mosques are fairly new. They were all constructed in -- from the 1970s onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is one mosque in Mehurici and one mosque in Zagradje proper?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to take you to the 314th Motorised Brigade and its establishment in late 1992. Is it correct that the Patriotic League in Gluha Bukovica joined the 314th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I only know that a company from the Gluha Bukovica Detachment became integrated in the 314th Motorised Brigade. As for the Patriotic League, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there also from Skomorje a unit which joined the 314th Brigade in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zagradje, Skomorje were the villages that became part of the Zagradje Company. And the Zagradje Company, members were members of the 314th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these two units you just mentioned, together with your Zagradje unit, they formed the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, no, those were not two units. Zagradje and Skomorje was just one unit. If you look at Gluha Bukovica and Zagradje, those were two companies by establishment. We called them companies at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these two companies you just referred to, did they form the 4th Battalion? You said already that this -- the headquarters of the 4th Battalion was in Gluha Bukovica?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zagradje -- you stated that you had been in the suburb of Luka or the hamlet of Luka in the Zagradje school. From when to when did you be the commander of the unit in the Luka school?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: From the 1st December 1992 until the 11th of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the 11th of May 1993, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of May 1993, pursuant to an order of the commander of the 314th Motorised Brigade, I was appointed the assistant commander for intelligence in the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from then onwards, from 11 May onwards, you were stationed again in Luka, or you moved to Gluha Bukovica where the headquarters of the 4th Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No. The man who was ordered to become the unit commander needed help, and I stayed on to help him in his new duty. From time to time, I would go to the defence line. I would report to the battalion command, and I would go back to the command of my unit, the unit that I was the commander of prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the unit you were commander of prior to that, this unit you were referring to, the Zagradje or Luka school unit, just for clarification?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. You just stated that you returned back to the command of my unit, the unit that I was commander of prior to that. I'm reading from the transcript here. I just wanted to establish, after 11th of May 1993, where were you, so to speak, based? Was this still in Luka school?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had received a task from the battalion commander. I was appointed to that duty, and I performed those duties. However, I still helped the new company commander. Why? Because I had received some education about tactics, about strategy, and since we were fortifying our defence lines and since the men trusted me as their commander and they obeyed me when it came to the performance of tasks, I remained there to help fortify the defence line. And also, from time to time, I would send intelligence on the enemy forces to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to take you now to the period in spring 1993 and talk again about this unit in the Luka school. You testified earlier it was an intervention unit. Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what the tasks of an intervention unit is, or what the tasks are?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: It was not a unit. We just call it a unit. However, it was a group of men, some 10 or so men, maybe between 10 and 15 soldiers, whose task was to intervene. In case we received information from the defence line which was along the Jesenica/Studenjacija river, their task was to go to the defence line in the shortest possible line and to preserve the line Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond occupied by the members of the 314th Brigade during that period of time. That was the task of that unit, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that this intervention unit, the 15 men you mentioned, they were engaging in hazardous tasks, dangerous tasks, being one of the first units who would go to the front line or who would be the front of the attack?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the armament --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, although the witness has answered, I would still object to this line of questioning. The witness has already said that in case this group was needed, they would be sent to the line. The witness did not mention any hazardous situations. The witness has answered. However, I just wanted to make it straight for the record. I wanted my objection to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection has been recorded. What has the Prosecution got to tell us with regard to this objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just, please tell me what the armament of your unit was.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I believe that I've already said that our unit had hunting rifles. Hunting rifles and carbines. Those were the type of weapons that the villagers had licenses for. Those licenses were obtained from the MUP in the Municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A witness testified in front of this Trial Chamber, Mr. Ribo, that towards the end of 1992, five or six mujahedin arrived in the school in Luka or Zagradje. Since your unit had been billeted in this school, have you seen these people?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: What period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo testified at the end of 1992. Page 11090 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: They were moving around the entire area. And Ribo could see them because Ribo's house is some 50 to 70 metres away from the school, whereas my house is about a kilometre away from the school. So Ribo could have seen these people in the schoolyard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were referring to Ribo's house, just for clarification? The transcript is not precise on this point here. You're referring to Ribo's house which is 50 metres away?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Ribo's house was between 50 and 70 metres away from the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 18 of the transcript, you're referring not necessarily to the mujahedin in Zagradje, but I believe you were referring to mujahedin in Mehurici, that some lads, I believe you were referring to locals, some locals joined the mujahedin for training. Can you elaborate a little bit on this.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: They had money. You have to bear that in mind. They also had uniforms, all sorts of uniforms, representing various armies of the world. They also had the humanitarian aspect. When I say that, I mean food. The young people who were still minors and not members of any of the BiH Army unit could not be mobilised by the Travnik Municipality staff. These young men went there to receive religious education-- primarily religious education, and they participated in the training as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said "these young men." Having lived in the Bila Valley your whole life, do you know any names of persons, of these young men?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Who are you referring to? The ones who underwent training?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the ones who underwent training with the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I know just one name. His -- this man's name was Avdija. He hailed from my village. His name was Avdija. And he received training, both religious training and training of other type.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Avdija, do you know a last name, please?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Kadric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did he receive that training, please?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I think that it was in 1993, mid-1993, June, July, August. During that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from the religious training you mentioned, he received also other training. What do you mean by "other training"?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, look, he received religious training. But apart from that training, they were trained in other fields. They received physical training. They ran through the villages. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They ran through villages. Through which villages? Where did the training of your neighbour take place?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, they weren't our neighbours. If we're using military terms, well, then, to the left and right we have neighbours. But I didn't have any neighbours there. If we use other terms, if we talk about it in other terms, they did pass through Mehurici, for example, and other inhabited places. They would go there before the religious service when there were a lot of people.
