utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So before the religious service, the mujahedin spoke to people and asked them - I'm just asking for clarification; I don't want to put words in your mouth - they were asking people whether they would join in training, or how did this work?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Look, everyone was free to express their opinion, to say whether they would join them or not. But since the population in the Bila Valley was in a crisis, the Bila Valley was in a crisis, the people weren't employed, there was nothing to eat, nothing to wear. And they used money and humanitarian aid to gain the support of these young men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me for the record, where did they usually make their approaches of the local population? Was this in front of the mosques or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I never had the opportunity of listening to any of them because I didn't like them much. But I assume that they approached the people who were present in the mosques.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the physician training Avdija Kadric received, would you call this a military training, or was it purely physical exercise?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was purely physical exercise. The people wore civilian clothes. If they had been involved in military exercises, they would have been -- they would have worn military uniforms. That was not the case when I saw them. After the training had been completed, they would then receive uniforms as a kind of prize.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, Avdija Kadric, did he stay with the mujahedin, or did he return to a regular ABiH unit?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the witness already said that this person was a young man who hadn't yet been mobilised, I think he has already answered this question, and I don't think the Prosecution can put the same question to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the age of Mr. Avdija Kadric in 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the training, did Mr. Kadric join any regular ABiH unit?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You should ask him. I don't know which units men were members of. Everyone was able to choose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the mujahedin stayed in the Mehurici elementary school and that at some point in time they went to Poljanice. Do you recall at what point in time they went to Poljanice? What month?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: They never went to Poljanice. I said they were in Savica Kuca, Savica houses. And as to when they left, I think it was towards the end of 1992 and at the beginning of 1993. That's when they left the primary school. But occasionally -- they apparently had premises of their own. And occasionally, one or two men would use those premises, would use that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now going to put a couple of names to you. Previous witnesses have testified that these people were in one way another affiliated with the mujahedin. Since you have lived in the area, I just want to ask whether you know these persons. Do you know Osman Tahirovic?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Osman Tahirovic -- you're asking me whether he was an inhabitant of the Bila -- I'm not sure which village you're referring to. Are you referring to my place, to my village? In that case, the local commune and the inhabitants of that local commune, well, I know there were three men with the same name in that local commune. I don't know who you're referring to, if it concerns some other Tahirovic, someone who arrived there. Before you said there were some Hamid Suljics in the area, too. If that is the case, it's difficult to say who this person was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witnesses said he worked in a cafe in Mehurici and that he cooked at the Mehurici school for the mujahedin. Maybe this helps you.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No. I never observed anything like this. As far as cafes are concerned, I was brought up in a religious way. And as a result, I rarely go to such places. If they had gone to a cake shop, perhaps I would have seen them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know any person by the name of Osman Tahirovic? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Look, I know three persons called Osman Tahirovic. So who is this person? Is this one of the three, or is it some other Tahirovic? I really don't know. Have you got a photograph of this person? If you do, then I'll have a look at it to see if I can remember such a person. But if not, I don't know how I can help you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any of the three Osman Tahirovics, was any of these three in the Muslimanske Snage in 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of Muslim forces being present there in 1992. I'm not aware of any presence of Muslim forces in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness already answered the question. But I think that the witness should first be asked of whether he is aware of the existence of Muslim forces. The Prosecution should establish the grounds upon which it wants to put its questions to the witness. But the witness has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Ramo Durmic?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I know the name. This is a name that one would hear. But I never saw him, and I wouldn't want to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jasarevic, do you know a person by the name of Vahid Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The Jasarevici live in Jezerci, if I remember this correctly. There are Jasarevics in Jezerci. I know someone called Vahid. Perhaps that's the person, a fat man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on to the incidents in Miletici on 24 April. You said you were at the forward command post on the 24th of April, and you returned to Mehurici. At what time in the day did you return to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: It was in the evening. I don't know the exact time. But it was already dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said together with another person -- a person drove you towards Luka, so you were sitting in a car before you were encountering the column of captives from Miletici. What was the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Look, first of all, I didn't go to Luka. I set off from Mehurici in the direction of Luka. In the area of Celamov Gaj, that's what we call the place, I came across this column. And the person I set off with was either Semir or Samir from Fazlic. He had a car. And he continued towards his place, whereas I stayed on there for about 15 minutes and then returned in the direction of the Mehurici school. So on that occasion, I didn't go to Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were on your way with Samir from Fazlic, when you were on your way to Celamov Gaj, did a car pass you from the opposite direction?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you finally encountered the column on Celamov Gaj, how broad was the street you were driving on? What was -- how broad was the street?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: How wide was it? Well, it wasn't a street. It was a -- it was a road. Perhaps it was 4 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were --

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: It was a dirt road, but it has now been asphalted. It's now an asphalt road. It's about 3 metres wide. And on both sides, there's perhaps a hard shoulder, which is about half a metre wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were sitting -- and this is actually a question. You were sitting next to the driver on the right-hand side when the column approached you?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Look, after about 20 minutes, we got out of the car -- after about 20 metres we got out of the car. The car was parked on the left-hand side, or rather on the right-hand side when coming from above. Across the road, there's the house belonging to the Ajanovic. So we parked -- the car was parked across the road from the house of Ajanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were outside the car while the column was passing, and it was already dark?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: While the column was passing by, I was at a distance of 2 or 3 metres from that column. It was on the left-hand side, or rather on the right-hand side if you come from above. So it passed by us on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the escorters, the first two persons of the escorters, were wearing automatic rifles and had masks. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, look, they had some sort of camouflage paint on them. I saw two them of with such paint on them. And those who were at the rear had these masks, and you could only see their eyes and to an extent it was possible to see their noses, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So altogether, how many escorters did you see?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I saw the first two men, and at the rear there were two or three men. But later when I wanted to react in some way when I saw that the father was covered in blood, I wanted to affront [as interpreted] them. I was then stopped by someone behind me who said "Suljic, we'll die, we'll be killed." He grabbed hold of my shoulder and said this. As I was afraid at the time, I couldn't tell you how many of them there were exactly. But I thought that there were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question: Was your impression that the escorters were exclusively foreigners, or could it also be that the escorters were locals?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, look, given the way that they spoke to each other, well, they were speaking in some foreign language that I couldn't identify, that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you returned to Mehurici, to the Mehurici school. Did you return by foot after you had waited the 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Look, first of all, I didn't go to the school. I returned on foot, and I went to the school's yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that an Emir was not available from the mujahedin at the beginning. Do you know who this Emir was, what the name of this Emir was? Did anybody mention the name of this Emir?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not sure whether there was an error in the translation. As far as I remember, the witness said that when he arrived there, there was no commander of the Siprage -- there was no unit commander of the Siprage Battalion. I don't remember the witness mentioning an Emir who was a mujahedin. I could check the transcript, but I don't think that the witness mentioned such an Emir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you should check this. But as far as I can remember, the witness did mention an Emir. And as I have a very good memory, he referred to an Emir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Without having verified it, while the witness was speaking, I believe it was on page 23, around line 19. Line 14, page 23. Am I allowed to ask the question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Should I repeat the question. I was asking for the name of the Emir, if you recall the name of the Emir from the mujahedin unit.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Are you referring to the person with whom they negotiated?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We just checked this part of the answer. The witness said that they tried to -- he said that it was difficult to establish contact with the Emir. And he said that he didn't know who that Emir was. I apologise if I did not accurately remember the answer this witness provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I return to the negotiations, can you just state for the record, next to Mr. Ribo, who was the name of the commander of the battalion in Mehurici who was involved in the negotiations? Just the name, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Look, at the time, I wasn't in a position to know anything about the battalion command of another unit. As a commander of the unit, I was an assistant commander for information and reconnaissance. And as such, I wasn't interested in the command of other units. And at that time, I didn't even know who the commander of my brigade was, let alone who people from other units were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the captured persons were released at night and transferred by bus to Luka, how many ABiH soldiers remained in Mehurici after the captives had been brought to Luka? How many soldiers approximately were there in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Look, there weren't any soldiers in Mehurici. There were three, four, or five men who were securing the facility where the unit command was located. All the men were at the defence lines, or they were involved in carrying out other tasks assigned to them by the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, while you were in Mehurici, did anybody ask for reinforcements to get new soldiers deployed to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I wasn't the commander of the units in the area of the Bila Valley, so I wasn't in a position to have all the information that concerned that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it maybe discussed to go and look in Gornji Miletici, to look for the remaining people there after the captured people from the mujahedin camp had been freed? Was it discussed to go and look in Gornji Miletici, what happened to the other persons?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, I don't know what the commanders of other units agreed on. From local people, I heard that they had asked the men in the command to protect the people first of all. And only after having provided protection for the people were they to provide protection for property. I don't know if they remained up there in Miletici. I wasn't aware of that. Later when I returned to Luka, I found out that some had remained up there in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day when Mr. Merdan was coming, do you recall the time of the day when Mr. Merdan was arriving?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's not possible to ask this witness such a question because the witness said that a BH Army officer came and introduced himself as Dzemal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned a while ago a person by the name of Dzemal. Do you know the last name of that person?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't. He didn't tell me what his last name was. All he said was that his name was Dzemal, and there was someone else with an HVO insignia on him. That's the first time I saw the HVO insignia. They said that they were from some sort of a joint command, and they said that they had to establish what had happened at the site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time of the 25th of April did you meet the person by the name of Dzemal?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact time. But I think it was in the middle of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then started, since this person told you to guard Gornji Miletici, you then started with the guarding. Until when -- when did you first start? Was it directly on that day that you started guarding Gornji Miletici? Or was it a day later?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No. Look, I hadn't been authorised by anyone to provide security for that village, nor had I been ordered to do so. However, the unit that was present in the area, I ordered the unit or that group of people, that group of men who were in the school to aid the people who had arrived in the area of Luka. Why did I do this? Because we thought that these people might appear again, and naturally the locals and these 15 soldiers tried to organise defence for that part of the population that had been brought there from the mujahedin camp. After Dzemal had arrived, he gave me the task of setting up a checkpoint. We were not to allow anyone to enter the village. And naturally, he also said that the people should be protected and that the village up there should be protected to the extent that this was possible. However, it wasn't possible to provide much protection because it's a very big area, and with 15 men, you could only hold a position about 200 metres long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification purposes, so you started the guarding on the 25th of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I started after having received this oral order from Dzemal. From that moment on, I assigned tasks. I positioned people, and I told them to provide security for the people and for the village as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when approximately did you supervise or perform these guard duties, until when?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to give you an approximation. We received the task, and it covered a certain period. And the period was up to the moment the vehicles came to transport the bodies from Miletici. And once the villagers of Miletici left, we stopped guarding them. The men who had stayed behind or the people who had stayed behind were taken over by the Ministry of the Interior. We, ourselves, returned to our everyday tasks, and we focussed our activities on the facilities which were on our defence lines between the two rivers, the Studenjacija and Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time your men or you yourself guarded the village of Gornji Miletici, was there any investigative activity carried out by others, by an ABiH unit in Gornji Miletici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not in a position to know everything. A foot soldier knows very little. It is more up to the man in charge to have such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other senior ABiH people enter the village of Miletici during the time you or your men were guarding? Did anybody enter the village apart from the inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I know that nobody but Dzemal did. Dzemal was the one who entered the village, together with us. And if you're referring to this soldier, he did. And also, some men of the 314th Brigade entered. As for the others, I don't know. I don't know if anybody else entered the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Merdan -- excuse me. I rephrase. Did Dzemal, who appeared on the 25th of April, ask you or in your presence anybody else about the mujahedin, whether the mujahedin had done anything in this village? Did he mention the mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't mention the mujahedin to me. So I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask you anything about your knowledge, since you were on the ground by the time? Did he want to know anything about the incident from your side?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't ask me. He only asked me to go to the spot with him. I was the unit commander. And he asked some other men to accompany us, for all of us to establish what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade wasn't in the area, I understand, in the area of the Bila Valley. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified -- I believe it was on transcript page 34, line 17 or 22, that the 7th -- members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade never were -- wore any insignia that would relate them to the army. Can you elaborate on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't think that the witness has ever said that in this particular way. He only said that he did not notice anybody wearing the insignia. He didn't say that members of this brigade didn't wear them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on page 21, just for the clarification. Page 34, line 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I can just read it for the record, the question was: "I'm referring to that specific event when you encountered that column. Did you notice or observe any members of the 7th Brigade?" The answer: "No, I didn't. I don't know that they were ever there. They would have had some insignia. These persons did not bear any insignia that related them to any Army."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, having read it again, I understood that you were referring to the escorters, is that correct, while stating this? This, rather, referred to the escorters of the column? Is that correct, just for clarification purposes?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: When you see your father who had been beaten and when you see him covered in blood, to ask you to look at the insignia and recognise the insignia, it's impossible. I was -- I was not in a position to see any insignia or recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have one last question; I move on to another topic. You said you were a member of the 314th Brigade in 1993, and you said that on the 11th of May 1993, you were an assistant commander for intelligence, if I recall correctly. Have you ever in 1993 been in any other unit than the 314th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any re-examination by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We don't have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No re-examination on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions to put to you, sir. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to go back to the incident involving your father. His name is Akif. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is Dedo Suljic?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: That is my uncle. My father's brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. In the column, you said that there was your father. Was his brother, Dedo, also there in the column?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the time? You said that it was in the afternoon. Could you be more specific and tell us what the time was when you encountered the column? As far as you can remember.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I remember that it was before the evening prayer, as we would say in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the time?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. One would have to check when the sunset was, and then we would know the exact time of the evening prayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you saw your father in the column, were his hands tied? Did you notice that detail or not?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, his hands were tied, both his hands and my uncle's hands were tied. Only Haso was free because he had a cane in his hands. He was an elderly person. That's why his hands were not tied. He could walk freely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your father, you spoke to him, and did he ever tell you why he was taken in that column together with the others?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I tried to establish some sort of contact with my father. I tried to receive some sort of information as to what had happened. However, my father never, ever discussed it, never wanted to talk about it. He only told me: "My child, it was down to the evil that had occurred." And that's the long and the short of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about your uncle, Dedo? Did he know any of the mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You should ask him that. I spent very little time in Miletici during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what would you say about the testimony of a previous witness who has told us about what had happened, and he said that -- that the mujahedin had arrived, and this is what had happened. And thereafter, according to the witness, your father and Dedo were the ones who came to see their friends. At that moment, there was shooting, and all the villagers were asked to gather in the square. Would your father remember that? Would your father remember the incident as it was described by a witness, that the mujahedin came to see their girlfriends and there was shooting, and that's how it all happened?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I've already told you what my father said. He never wanted to discuss those things. My opinion is that he had been hit by one of those masked men. He was hit in the forehead, and he still suffers consequences. I'm sure that he was afraid that if he had told me, I would try and do something. And for that reason, he never wanted to discuss those things. As for the statements of different witnesses, whatever somebody tells me, somebody may guarantee that I would be safe and that I will go back home safely. However, accidents happen, and one can never be a hundred per cent sure of what will happen or what will not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your answer is -- has two parts. The first part is that your father never spoke with you about the things that happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: My father has never spoken about that. However, what he told me, as I've already told you, was that evil things had happened, and he told me: "My dear child, the evil had happened." And since we were so close, they will say that it was the neighbours who did it. And this was my interpretation of his words, the words that he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the second part of your answer you said that accidents may happen. Am I to understand that you are afraid, having testified here?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, no. Why would I be afraid? I am here to tell you what I saw and to tell you the truth. Now, as to what other people said, I cannot confirm or deny that because I was not in the same place where that other person was. I have told you what I know, and this is the only thing that I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Moving on to another subject, the school in Zagradje, if I've understood you well, your unit was billeted in that school.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: The command and some of the troops were there. This intervention platoon was there. The rest of the unit was on the defence lines facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has asked you about Mr. Ribo, who saw the mujahedin in the school in Zagradje. And you said that you yourself never saw them there. There is also another testimony present before this Trial Chamber which indicates that there were mujahedin in that school. My question to you is as follows: Were there the mujahedin in the Zagradje school, the mujahedin who had arrived, who maybe stayed there, who had an office there? Or can you confirm that you never saw them there?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: During the period while I was the unit commander, the company commander, they did arrive in the perimeter of the school. They arrived in a white Toyota. After the time when I was wounded, on the 8th of June 1993 up to the end of 1993, I did not have any contacts either with my unit or with the battalion command. I was in the hospital in Zenica. During that period of time, maybe somebody was there, but I wouldn't know because I didn't see them. Maybe your other witnesses did see them and told you what they saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that one day, they arrived in a white Toyota, and that they stopped in the school's yard. What did they do there?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They just made a U-turn in that white Toyota. Behind the school, they made a U-turn, and they returned. I was in front of the school. There is a plateau and a little wall. We were sitting on that wall. We were smoking and talking. They made a U-turn in front of that school, and that's when I saw this car, the white car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were they armed when they were in that white car? The mujahedin, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I did not see whether they were armed or not. I only saw that one person drove this Toyota.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he on his own, or were there any others with him?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I saw only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another topic: The Prosecution has indicated to you, and you confirmed this spontaneously, that Avdija Kadric, whose age you don't know, underwent training with the mujahedin. This Avdija Kadric, did you ever see him again after the year 1993? Or has he completely gone from the area? Has he gone missing, or does he still reside in the area?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Avdija Kadric was a very restless person and a very courageous person. He was a good fighter. It was very difficult to control him. He had a different feeling for the fight, different than any other member of the unit. Currently, he's not in the area because he died in Meokrnje in 1994 together with the other men who were in combat, who were involved in the combat activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that he got killed in 1994 during combat?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I am not sure of the year, but it was during the Meokrnje operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he a member of a regular unit when he was killed? Was he a regular fighter?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What unit was that?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was a member of the 306th at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that in 1994, he was killed in combat while he was a member of the 306th.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the year. But I know that he was a member of that unit at the time, and that he was killed in -- on this mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that you finished the school for reserve officers in the former JNA and that you were given the rank of captain. So you did have a military rank. According to your knowledge, in the years 1992 and 1993, men aged 18 and onwards, did they have to be mobilised into the units of the BH Army because of the state of the war that was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: First of all, when I left the JNA, I was not a captain. In order to become captain, you had to go to school for four to six years. Secondly, in the JNA, I was a foot soldier. I finished the reserve officers' school. But when you finish that, you are either a lance corporal or a corporal, which means that you could only command over a unit of ten soldiers. Once I left Bileca, I went to Pancevo, and then to Sombor, and after that I was given the rank of a lance corporal. As for the rank of captain, I gained that during the war, between 1992 and 1996. To be more precise, in the year 1994, because all the other officers of the BiH Army were promoted, and pursuant to that I was given the rank of captain in the BiH Army. When we're talking about young people aged 18 and older, there was no obligation. Nobody could force anybody of age to be a member of the BH Army. You could also not force an elderly person, a person who was not fit for service, to fight in the war. There was a decision of the presidency stating exactly how old mobilised members of the BH Army should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, according to you, there was no obligation for the people aged 18 and older to become members of the army.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, there was no such obligation. Those who were younger than 18 were not obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But those who were older than 18, they were obliged to become members of the army? They had to be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they fell under the obligation to be mobilised. That was pursuant to the decision of the Presidency proclaiming the state of war, and it was the duty of every citizen of the state to defend their country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question before the break. You have told us that you were guarding the village of Miletici, and you were present in Miletici. The Prosecution has asked you that, but there were some other persons who were responsible for that. I would like to know the following: When you were mounting guard in Miletici, was there anybody above you who was there who had a higher rank, or were you the only officer with some sort of authority who was in charge of providing security for Miletici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, there were no ranks in the BiH Army. There were just markings. There was a blue mark and a yellow mark. The yellow mark designated commanders. The blue mark was for the persons who did not have the authority to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was your colour?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I wore the colour yellow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. In Miletici, were there other persons with the yellow colour, or were you the only ones wearing this yellow colour, the yellow marking?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: There were platoon commanders. Some of them were on the lines, and one of them was in the school in Luka. Platoon commanders had the same yellow markings, however their bands were somewhat narrower than mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The platoon commander who was in the school -- was there a military police platoon there or not?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: You mean in the school in Zagradje or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No. In the Zagradje school, there was never a military police platoon, or at least I don't remember police being there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were in Miletici, if a crime had been committed, who would have carried out an investigation into that crime?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know who would be in charge. I believe it would be the Ministry of the Interior and those who were dealing in those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's imagine a situation. For example, your soldier, a soldier under you was in combat, and there was a mutual wounding, and there should have been an investigation. Who would decide on the investigation that would be carried out? Who had the authority to order an investigation?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, none of my soldiers were involved in mutual -- in an accident of that sort. However, if a soldier would be involved, the investigation would be carried out by a military body, maybe the security body. If the persons involved were civilians, then it would be the civilian police who would carry out such an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you very much. It is half past 12.00. We are -- we should resume at 5 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume. The Judges have a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Very few short questions on the events in Miletici in April 1993. I understand you were born and you lived during your childhood in Miletici itself.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I was born in Zagradje, 25th of April 1970. In 1972, my family bought some land and moved to Donji Miletici, so I was very young when we arrived in Miletici. However, I was born in Zagradje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: This was Donji Miletici, you said, yes. And this was the Muslim part of the village, and you had a Gornji Miletici, and that was the Croat part. That is right?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Donji Miletici, before we bought that land I mentioned, there were Croats who were living there. We bought their land, and after they had sold their property they moved to Nova Bila, to Stara Bila. They moved to that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If you go from Mehurici to Miletici, or if you go from Luka to Miletici from Zagradje, you pass first Gornji Miletici, and then you come into -- you pass first Donji Miletici and then you come into Gornji Miletici, or is it the other way around?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: If you go to Miletici from Mehurici, it's about 2 or 3 kilometres away. And you go along -- you go by the road along the Jasenica River. When you reach Luka, there is a road for Miletici. To the right, there is the road leading to the Miletici, and to the left is the road leading to Luka or rather, to the bridge and then to Zagradje. To the right you have the road leading to Miletici. You reach Donji Miletici as you said. That's where we were. That's where we lived. And then the bend, the road leads to Gornji Miletici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So if you want to go to Miletici from Mehurici, you have to pass Luka, or practically pass Luka. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: If you are driving, you have to drive by Luka. If you go on foot, there are a number of routes from Mehurici that can be used. From the crossing for Fazlici and Jezerci, at that crossing there is a village path that the locals used to use to descend from Gornji and Donji Miletici and to reach Mehurici. You can also leave Donji Miletici and descend to the road to Jasenica, so there are a number of village paths. If you drive, then the only possible way of reaching that place is via Luka and Donji Miletici and then you reach Gornji Miletici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If understand from your -- what you have said this morning, that the mujahedin must have taken the main road. Is that right? Because there you met on the main road.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they used the main road, that's true. I met them in Celamov Gaj. That's on the main road to Mehurici. How should I say it? To Mehurici and Zagradje. And below the bend, which is where I met them, there is a road that leads to Fazlici and to Jezerci. That's the main road which leads to Skomorje, Zagradje, Miletici, Jezerci, Fazlici, that's the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If they would have taken the main road by going to Miletici, they would have passed the house of your uncle and your father before coming to the Croat houses. Is that correct also?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Who are you referring to? The mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The group you met on its way to Mehurici. If they would have gone to Miletici to take these people away, they would have passed your uncle's house or your father's house before coming to the Croat part. I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the route the mujahedin used to enter the village. But the column was moving in the direction of Gornji Miletici. They passed by Donji Miletici. They passed by the bend that leads to Fazlici. At that bend, there is a road, a sort of footpath, towards Fazlici. And then there's Celamov Gaj, and they used that road to Celamov Gaj to reach the main road below the tunnel. And I could see them there on that main road. They didn't go around, via Luka. That's not the route they used to escort those people from Miletici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you lived in Donji Miletici for a long time, I will ask you the name of some witnesses mentioned. Do you know a family with the name Kasimov in Donji Miletici, or perhaps Kasumovic? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Look, Kasumovic, no, I don't know that name, that family name. There was no one that had that family name in Miletici. In Donji Miletici, after the Croats had left, when we bought the land, that was in the 1970s, there were only four brothers living there. Their name was Suljic. So there was no one by the name of Kasumovic, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I was just asking you because I stumbled across the name in some document. And you say there is no family with such a name. No Dedo Kasimov either?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No. Not in that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps you know, and you may not know - I'm not sure what you know and what you don't know - but what I'm interested in is to know why the mujahedin went to Miletici in the first place? What was their purpose in going to Miletici? Have you ever heard an explanation for their going to that village?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard such an explanation. And I can't say anything about that since I don't know. I can only tell you about what I saw. But as to what I heard, as to what other people said, I can't take such information to be credible. All I can do is tell you about what I personally saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You can't know what you don't know. My last question relates to your meeting the column of these armed mujahedin and these prisoners, among them your father. Was it still light when you met them, or was it becoming dark? Or have you any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, on the whole, it was visible. I recognised my father and those neighbours in the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said that the mujahedin on the front of the group had painted faces. And afterwards, at the end of the group, you saw mujahedin with masks. And in between were the prisoners, so to speak. Did you also observe how they were clothed? Do you remember their clothes, things they wore?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the civilians or the men who were masked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, not the prisoners; their escorts.

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, look, they were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said you were not able to distinguish any insignia on their uniforms. So you could not tell what kind of people they were in that respect. Did you see them wearing or some of them wearing some band on their arms, or not?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them wearing bands on their arms. They didn't have any bands. They didn't have any armbands on. The only thing I noticed was a sort of green ribbon on their caps, so I don't know if that has any significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And caps, that means masks, or is that something else, then?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to these balaclavas that had an opening for their eyes and mouths, and they had sort of a ribbon on those masks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: One witness has said, now that you are mentioning balaclavas, they had nylon masks. Have you seen that also?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I think you said before this morning that there were four or five mujahedin, or four or five escorts, not more than four or five. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I saw two at the front and two or three at the rear. I couldn't see how many other men there were, but on both sides there were men providing security, or rather, men escorting the people to the place they wanted to take them to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said that your father didn't want to discuss the events with you because it was apparently too painful for him to do. Did you discuss them -- the events with your uncle, Dedo, for instance, or with your other family members? I forgot his first name at the moment, but your uncle's uncle was also part of the story. Did you discuss the events with other family members who were present?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say. This was a subject that was discussed, but I was not interested in it. So I didn't feel the need to listen to what the man had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I've just one question. Further cross-examined by Mr. Neuner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You responded to Judge Swart that if a car would go from Miletici to Mehurici, it would need to take the road along the River Jasenica. And you were on that road when you encountered the column. Witnesses testified before this Trial Chamber that one Croat woman from Miletici was wounded during the incident on the 24th of April 1993 in Gornji Miletici. And she couldn't walk. She, therefore, had to be brought by a car to Mehurici. You said before you encountered the column of walking captives from Gornji Miletici you hadn't seen a car. But once you remained on the road and walked back to Mehurici, did there a car pass by?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember there being any cars. But I heard that the wounded woman was taken to Mehurici. I really didn't see how she was taken there. I didn't really see the form of transport used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the road you took towards Donji Miletici that evening when it was already dark, there was no car coming in the opposite direction before you met the column and after you met the column?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any cars. I can't remember any cars. Perhaps there were some. But at the time, I don't remember there being any vehicles of any kind on that road from Mehurici-Celamov Gaj. Later when I went down to Mehurici, naturally there were cars passing by, but I wasn't really interested in who these cars belonged to or the type of cars. What I was interested in was to know where my father had gone. I wanted to know where they had taken him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only alternative road from the road you took would have been, then, a footpath. Do I understand this correctly, a footpath which could be taken maybe also by a car, a footpath on the other side of the river?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: There's no path on the other side of the river. There's one path -- there's one road for vehicles. That's all on the side where the road is. The road is on the right side if you are coming from Mehurici. It's on the right side of the river, on the right bank. It goes along the river. And that's the road that could be used to reach Miletici. And as to the routes used by the inhabitants to get down to Mehurici, well, only -- this was only used by people who went on foot or by horses because horses were used to transport flour, sugar and oil at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Further examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Suljic, how far is the place where you met the column from Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, if you set off from the bridge, then it's between four and five hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long does it take to reach that place in a car, to reach that place from Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, you could get there in two minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned colleague asked you whether you had seen a vehicle of any kind. You didn't see any vehicles from the time you left Miletici or Mehurici until the time when you returned to Mehurici. What sort of a time period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, from the time I left the bridge, it was about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know whether any vehicles used that road either before or after that period?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that. I didn't use the road used by cars to return. There is a path. Before you enter Mehurici, you turn right, and then you cross a small bridge. And that is the shortcut I used to reach the school. Perhaps while I was going along that path, some vehicle passed by. But during that period, I didn't notice anything. I didn't see any vehicles apart from my one that headed off to the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it's clear now. You said that you were the commander of a company of the 4th Battalion in the 314th Brigade. When were you appointed to that duty?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of December 1992. That's when an order was issued by the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 1st of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The last question which was just asked didn't arise out of the Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What is the purpose of the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you asked the witness when he was in the primary school in Zagradje, you asked him whether he had seen the mujahedin. That's why I want him to specify the time when he was in the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, from the 1st of December up until the 8th of June when you were wounded, and as you said, was that the period during which you had your headquarters in the school in Zagradje, in Luka?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's where the unit command was located. But I wasn't there at all times. I spent more time at the defence lines than in the unit's command. The commander should be with his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But that's the period during which you occasionally spent time in the primary school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following -- or rather the next question that the Presiding Judge asked you had to do with mobilisation. After they had declared a state of war, who was to be mobilised? Were all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be mobilised, all those citizens of a certain age group, or were there some exceptions?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: A state of war had been declared, and a general mobilisation had been declared. So naturally, it was everyone's duty to report to the nearest unit. I can't remember the years concerned or the age group concerned. All I know is that minors were not to be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, given this general mobilisation, tell me whether the Serbian and Croatian population in your area joined the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, they didn't. And the neighbours -- my neighbours with whom I lived, were not members of the BH Army. I don't know if they became members of other formations at a later date, of other formations in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question I put to you, you mentioned the possibilities that the army and Territorial Defence had. Your brigade, or rather, your unit, were they in a position to provide soldiers with rifles, equipment, and other necessary items?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, this was not possible for us to do. We used what we had. There were hunting rifles. We had civilian clothes, clothes that the locals usually wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, you mentioned "company" on a number of occasions, and then you -- could you tell me whether it was possible to carry out an overall mobilisation and bring the units of the BH Army up to strength in terms of the establishment in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMID SULJIC
utterances.text: No, this was never possible. We referred to companies, battalions, and brigade. But to form a company of 50 men, well, such a unit is not a company.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this concludes your testimony. Thank you for having come to testify at The Hague. You have answered all the questions put to you. We wish you a good trip home, and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have the document. I'll give the floor to the Defence for our schedule for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have the witness who has been scheduled for tomorrow. He's on the list that we have provided to the Chamber. We'll be seeing the witness today. For the moment, he's not requesting protective measures of any kind. But we'll be able to tell you whether this is the case tomorrow. And I hope that we'll be able to conclude the examination of this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are there any other issues that either of the parties would like to raise given that we still have a few minutes left? Very well, in that case, we will now adjourn. I will see you all tomorrow at the hearing at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
